extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students (litigators handling patent invalidity/defense issues)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for litigating and proving common invalidity defenses to a patent (prior use, prior patent, prior publication, and want of utility), including evidence standards, burdens of proof, and how courts treat witness/expert testimony and foreign documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use may be proved though abandoned
rubrics_metrics.description: That prior use may be proved though the use has been abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior use is admissible even if the prior user abandoned the practice. Evidence of prior use is sufficient if it shows the invention existed and was known/used at the relevant time. However, the court weighs credibility (e.g., single witness testimony in a large town may be insufficient). Defendant bears the burden to prove prior use once the plaintiff's patent is in evidence; if defendant's proof leaves reasonable doubt the patent's prima facie novelty remains. See also distinctions when use is ancient or when models/machines are not extant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign reduction to practice / use limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: That evidence of reduction to practice abroad prior to invention in the United States is inadmissible; evidence of use abroad is not admissible (subject to nuances about foreign patents/publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of foreign reduction to practice or foreign use generally does not prove anticipation in U.S. litigation unless it meets the particular rules for foreign patents/public disclosure. Foreign machines not arriving in the U.S. until after the plaintiff's inventive act have no bearing on novelty. For foreign patents, defendant must show the patent was 'public' according to the law of its country and the date of its public disclosure. Treat foreign prior acts carefully: some foreign systems publish later, or keep patents secret, and the operative date for anticipation may be the date of publication, not grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency and credibility of witness testimony on prior use
rubrics_metrics.description: The testimony of witnesses as to the fact of use and the completeness and availability of the invention is generally reliable unless inconsistent with other events; single-witness testimony may not overcome presumptions from the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts assess witness credibility: honest witnesses' recollections about operativeness and employment of conceded articles are usually reliable, but statements inconsistent with general events or contradicted by negative witnesses weaken the proof. Silence or lack of attacks on a prior device may raise presumptions; intangible presumptions yield to positive proof. Positive evidence of existence/use outweighs mere negative testimony. Examples: testimony of one witness that a device was in use twenty years earlier may not be sufficient where many would have known of it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attack the identity or the use; compare inventions and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff rebutting a defendant's evidence of prior use may attack either the identity or the use of the prior art or article; superior utility of one invention may indicate an essential difference of means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show differences of identity, compare the two inventions, their practical operation, and acceptance by the public. Commercial success of one and failure of the other can indicate essential differences. Superior utility may be shown by direct comparison, operation results, or public acceptance. Courts may infer that large differences in effect imply substantial differences in means. Use of comparisons and demonstration of relative utility are legitimate rebuttal strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost art, abandonment, and negative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may show that an alleged prior invention was incomplete, inoperative, abandoned, or had become a 'lost art' before the plaintiff's inventive act; negative evidence (testimony that those who would have known of the use did not) is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff may prove prior device was inoperative or abandoned as an unsuccessful experiment; abandonment may be inferred from cessation of use where the invention would otherwise have utility. If the alleged prior art became a lost art that passed from public knowledge and was later rediscovered, that does not necessarily establish prior use. Negative testimony from persons who would have been acquainted with the invention if it had been used can contradict assertions of prior use. The court weighs such negative evidence heavily in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and effect of patent as prima facie evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent is prima facie evidence of novelty and utility; the burden of proof on novelty/utility defenses rests on the defendant, though the burden may shift in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plaintiff's patent carries a presumption of novelty and utility; the defendant must affirmatively prove anticipation by prior use, prior patent, or prior publication. When the defendant proves a use anterior to the plaintiff's application (especially if the prior existence is evidenced by a patent issued before the plaintiff's), the burden shifts to the plaintiff to prove an earlier inventive act. Where several prior inventions or patents are alleged, each must be separately considered and proved. If defendant's evidence fully meets the standard, novelty is impugned; otherwise the presumption stands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patent defense: identity and public issuance/date
rubrics_metrics.description: When novelty is denied on the ground of a prior patent, two questions arise: (1) whether the plaintiff's invention is identical with or included in the prior patent; (2) whether the prior patent was duly issued and publicly accessible before the plaintiff's conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defendant's primary evidence is the prior patent itself, construed alongside the plaintiff's patent; courts often use experts to compare claims and specifications. The defendant must show the prior patent was a public document under the issuing country's law and that it was published/made accessible before the plaintiff's inventive act. Certified copies from patent offices are prima facie evidence of existence, date, and contents; where foreign patents have different regimes (secret vs public), the defendant must prove which category applies. Re-issues, file wrappers, and similar materials have limitations and do not always show operative dates or reductions to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior publication defense: three requisites
rubrics_metrics.description: To invalidate a patent by prior publication the alleged publication must: (1) be a public work; (2) describe the invention so a person skilled in the art can practise it without further directions; (3) have been made accessible to the public before the plaintiff's conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts determine public character from contents, source, and intended audience (e.g., printed for unrestricted circulation, library cataloging, sale/distribution). Whether the description enables practice is shown by experts/practical mechanics who have constructed or attempted to construct from it. Accessibility must be proved by extrinsic evidence (imprint/title-page is not enough); proof methods include library records, sale/distribution testimony, catalogues, government lodging. If a copy cannot be produced, parol evidence of contents and date is allowed but considered weak and subject to credibility issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof that a specification/publication enables practice by skilled persons
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior patent or publication must be sufficiently precise and complete to enable persons skilled in the art to practise the invention without the exercise of their own inventive faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant should offer testimony from those who actually constructed and used the invention under guidance of the prior disclosure or from experts/practical workmen opining that the disclosure enabled practice. The plaintiff may offer counter-experts. The jury assesses credibility and weight; in cases of doubt the plaintiff prevails. Certificates or authenticated patent office copies support the defendant's proof of contents and date where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Want of utility (sixth defence) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The sixth defence denies the utility of the patented invention; the patent is prima facie evidence of utility and the defendant must prove uselessness beyond reasonable doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Available evidence includes expert testimony who, after inspection, find the device inutility, and testimony of practical mechanics who attempted to use it and found it worthless. If invention is shown to be mischievous or frivolous, defence can succeed. Plaintiff rebuts with experts, evidence of extensive use, commercial success, or proof of effect on the art. A defendant who has used the invention or obtained a patent for substantially the same art is estopped from denying utility. Courts ordinarily will not overturn Patent Office findings of utility lightly unless proof is strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and admissibility of evidence (certified copies, drawings, parol, experts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissible evidence includes certified copies of patents/specifications/drawings, specimens, sketches/drawings, witness testimony, experts, practical mechanics; but some items (e.g., file wrappers, title-page imprint) have limited probative value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certified patent office copies are prima facie proof of issue, date, and contents. Where copies are unobtainable, parol proof of publication and contents may be admitted but is weaker and subject to scrutiny. Experts are routinely used to explain/compare patent claims and to testify whether a disclosure enables practice. Negative evidence (witnesses who would have known but did not) and silence can create presumptions but yield to positive proof. Courts treat different evidence types with varying weight; documentary authenticated evidence is strongest.
